name: Eisenhower Matrix
description: Sorts the tasks or choices bound up in your question into four boxes by urgency and importance, so you can see what actually deserves your attention first.
whenToUse: Use when you're overwhelmed by competing tasks or options and need to decide what to act on now versus later.
origin: Popularized as the 'Time Management Matrix' by Stephen Covey in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989), built on a distinction Dwight D. Eisenhower drew in a 1954 speech at Northwestern University. Eisenhower himself credited the idea to an unnamed 'former college president,' and his actual words were: 'I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.' The now-common paraphrase — 'What is important is seldom urgent, and what is urgent is seldom important' — is a later, looser rendering that hardened into the standard quote; Eisenhower never said it verbatim, and he wasn't its original source either.
howToApply: List everything competing for your attention right now.
Ask whether each item is urgent — does it carry a hard deadline or an immediate consequence if you wait?
Ask whether each item is important — does it move you toward a goal or value you actually care about, independent of when it's due?
Sort each item into one of the four boxes: Do First, Schedule, Delegate, or Eliminate.
Act on Do First immediately, but treat Schedule as the real priority — Covey's point was that a starved Schedule box is what keeps generating more Do First crises.
Delegate or batch what you can, and consciously drop or ignore Eliminate rather than let it quietly fill your day.
pros: Extremely fast to apply, no special training needed.
Forces an explicit urgent-vs-important distinction most people blur.
Good antidote to constantly firefighting urgent-but-unimportant work.
Widely implemented in real tools (Todoist, dedicated apps like eisenhower.me), so the four-box vocabulary already travels well across teams.
cons: Binary low/high buckets hide real nuance — many tasks sit in between.
Says nothing about how to actually do the important work, just where to place it.
Easy to rationalize almost anything into 'urgent' under pressure.
The Delegate box assumes you have someone to delegate to — for solo work or individual contributors it often just becomes a second Do First.

example.scenario: Deciding how to spend a chaotic Monday: a client emergency, a strategy doc due Friday, a backlog of routine status emails, a teammate's request for 1:1 feedback on their draft, and an invitation to browse an industry newsletter.

quadrants.name: Do First
items: Resolve the client emergency

quadrants.name: Schedule
items: Draft the Friday strategy doc
Give the teammate real feedback on their draft

quadrants.name: Delegate
items: Clear the routine status email backlog

quadrants.name: Eliminate
items: Browse the industry newsletter

result.summary: Handle the client emergency now. Protect real blocks this week for the strategy doc and the teammate's feedback — that Schedule box is the one actually worth defending. Batch the routine emails, skip the newsletter.

name: SWOT Analysis
description: Breaks your question down into Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats.
whenToUse: Use when evaluating a plan, venture, or choice against both your own capabilities and the outside environment.
origin: Credited to Albert Humphrey and colleagues at the Stanford Research Institute in the 1960s-70s, developed while studying why corporate strategic planning consistently failed.
howToApply: Name the specific decision or venture you're evaluating.
List Strengths — internal advantages you already have.
List Weaknesses — internal gaps or disadvantages.
List Opportunities — external factors that could work in your favor.
List Threats — external factors that could work against you.
Look for pairings: which strengths let you capture which opportunities, and which weaknesses expose you to which threats.
pros: Simple four-box structure anyone can follow without training.
Forces you to look outward at the market or environment, not just inward.
Works at almost any scale — a single decision or a whole company.
cons: Produces a list, not a plan — nothing tells you what to do with the four boxes.
Easy to generate generic, interchangeable items that don't sharpen the decision.
No weighting — a minor strength sits next to a critical one with equal visual weight.

result.summary: Savings and network make this a viable bet, but build a business-basics plan before the safety net matters.

name: BCG Box
description: Plots the options or initiatives in your question on market growth versus relative share to see which deserve investment, which to hold, and which to drop.
whenToUse: Use when comparing multiple options, initiatives, or products for where to put limited resources.
origin: Developed by Bruce Henderson and the Boston Consulting Group in 1970 to help companies decide where to allocate cash across a portfolio of products.
howToApply: List the products, initiatives, or options you're comparing.
Estimate each one's relative market share (or your relative strength) — low or high.
Estimate each one's market growth (or momentum and opportunity) — low or high.
Place each in Star, Cash Cow, Question Mark, or Dog.
Invest in Stars, harvest Cash Cows, decide selectively on Question Marks, and consider dropping Dogs.
pros: Forces explicit prioritization instead of funding everything equally.
Good visual shorthand for portfolio-level conversations.
Highlights products quietly draining resources (Dogs) that habit keeps alive.
cons: Only two dimensions — ignores strategic fit, brand value, or synergy across products.
'Low/high' judgments are often subjective and easy to bend toward a preferred conclusion.
Designed for product portfolios, so it translates awkwardly to personal or non-market decisions.

name: Johari Window
description: Maps what's known and unknown to you and to others about the situation in your question, to surface blind spots.
whenToUse: Use when trying to understand yourself better, or close a gap between how you see yourself and how others see you.
origin: Developed in 1955 by psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham — the name blends their first names, 'Jo' and 'Harri'.
howToApply: Pick a specific trait, behavior, or situation you want to understand better.
Fill the Arena — what you know about yourself here and others also see.
Fill the Blind Spot — what others likely see that you don't recognize in yourself.
Fill the Facade — what you know about yourself but keep from others.
Fill the Unknown — what neither you nor others have surfaced yet.
Seek feedback to shrink the Blind Spot, and consider disclosure to shrink the Facade.
pros: One of the few models that explicitly surfaces blind spots — things you can't see about yourself by definition.
Encourages a concrete conversation about feedback and disclosure, not just abstract self-reflection.
Simple enough to redo periodically and track how the panes shift.
cons: The Blind Spot and Unknown panes are inherently hard to fill in without honest outside input.
Can feel exposing — some people resist naming their own Facade honestly.
Says nothing about how to act on what's uncovered.

quadrants.name: Blind Spot

quadrants.name: Facade

quadrants.name: Unknown
items: How your reaction to past pushback shaped the team's caution

result.summary: The Blind Spot is likely doing the most damage — ask a trusted colleague directly how your tone lands.

name: GROW Model (Whitmore)
description: Walks your question through Goal, Reality, Options, Will — John Whitmore's coaching model for moving from stuck to a concrete next action.
whenToUse: Use when coaching yourself or someone else through a specific goal or performance question.
origin: Developed in the UK in the late 1980s by Graham Alexander, Alan Fine, and Sir John Whitmore, and popularized through Whitmore's book 'Coaching for Performance'.
howToApply: Goal — define specifically what you or the person being coached wants to achieve.
Reality — honestly assess where things stand today relative to that goal.
Options — brainstorm possible paths forward without judging them yet.
Will — commit to a specific next action and a timeframe.
pros: Simple four-step structure that works in a single conversation.
Separates 'what do I want' from 'what will I do', preventing a jump straight to action without clarity.
Widely used and taught, so it's easy to find coaching partners who already know it.
cons: Assumes the goal is basically sound — doesn't question whether it's the right goal.
Can feel mechanical if run as a checklist rather than a real conversation.
Depends heavily on how well Reality is assessed — sugar-coating it undermines everything after.

steps.title: Options
steps.description: Volunteer to lead the next small project; ask for stretch feedback duties; find a mentor already in the role.

steps.title: Will
steps.description: Ask to lead the upcoming migration project starting next sprint.

result.summary: Owning a visible project is the fastest path from 'strong technically' to 'ready to lead'.

name: Pareto Principle
description: Identifies the small subset of factors in your question likely responsible for most of the outcome — the 80/20 view.
whenToUse: Use when you have many possible causes or actions and need to find the vital few worth focusing on.
origin: Named after economist Vilfredo Pareto, who observed in 1896 that roughly 80% of Italy's land was owned by 20% of the population; later generalized into the '80/20 rule' by quality theorist Joseph Juran.
howToApply: List every factor, cause, or task contributing to the outcome you care about.
Estimate how much each one actually contributes to the result.
Rank them from highest to lowest contribution.
Identify the small top slice responsible for most of the impact.
Focus effort there first, and deprioritize the long tail.
pros: Cuts through busywork by making you name what actually moves the needle.
Backed by a real, frequently observed pattern across many domains — sales, bugs, complaints.
Simple enough to apply to almost any list of competing priorities.
cons: The exact 80/20 split is a rough heuristic, not a law — real ratios vary a lot.
Estimating 'contribution' is often a guess, especially without real data.
Can wrongly justify ignoring the long tail entirely, when small items sometimes compound.

name: Cognitive Dissonance
description: Looks at the tension between conflicting beliefs, values, or actions embedded in your question, and how that discomfort might be shaping your thinking.
whenToUse: Use when you notice you're rationalizing a choice, or your stated values and actual behavior seem to conflict.
origin: Coined by psychologist Leon Festinger in his 1957 book 'A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance', based on his study of a doomsday cult whose members intensified belief after their prophecy publicly failed.
howToApply: Name the two or more beliefs, values, or actions that seem to conflict.
Notice the discomfort itself — dissonance usually shows up as unease, defensiveness, or over-justification.
Identify the rationalizations you're currently using to reduce that discomfort.
Ask what would actually resolve the conflict — changing the belief, the action, or your justification.
Choose deliberately rather than letting the rationalization quietly win by default.
pros: Explains a specific, common trap: justifying a choice after the fact instead of evaluating it honestly.
Helps you notice when you're arguing with yourself, not just deciding.
Applies broadly — decisions, relationships, habits, beliefs.
cons: Purely diagnostic — it names the tension but doesn't tell you which side should win.
Requires real self-honesty; it's easy to use the model itself as another rationalization.
Can be uncomfortable to sit with, which is exactly what makes people avoid doing it.

sections.heading: The Rationalization at Work

sections.heading: What Resolving It Would Require
sections.body: Either genuinely committing to use it, or admitting the purchase missed and adjusting future spending habits.

result.summary: The defensiveness is a signal, not noise — it's pointing at a purchase decision worth reassessing honestly.

name: SCAMPER
description: Generates fresh options for your question by forcing it through seven lenses: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse.
whenToUse: Use when you feel stuck on a decision and want to force fresh alternatives into view.
origin: Devised by Bob Eberle in 1971 as a mnemonic checklist, building on brainstorming techniques originated by advertising executive Alex Osborn.
howToApply: State the thing you're trying to improve or rethink.
Substitute — what could you swap out?
Combine — what could you merge with something else?
Adapt — what could you borrow from elsewhere?
Modify — what could you exaggerate, minimize, or change?
Put to another use — how else could this be used?
Eliminate — what could you remove entirely?
Reverse — what if you flipped it around?
pros: Seven distinct lenses force genuinely different angles instead of one more pass at the same idea.
Works well solo or in a group brainstorm.
Concrete letters make it easy to remember and reuse without notes.
cons: Not every lens fits every problem — some prompts produce forced, low-quality ideas.
Generates raw options, not evaluation — you still need a separate step to pick the good ones.
Can feel gimmicky if used mechanically rather than as a genuine creative prompt.

result.summary: Substitute and Eliminate score highest — the meeting itself may be the problem, not its format.

name: Project Portfolio Matrix
description: Plots the initiatives or options in your question by expected value against feasibility, so you can see which to pursue now, which need more groundwork, and which to drop.
whenToUse: Use when you're weighing several possible initiatives, projects, or investments and need to prioritize which to fund first.
origin: A staple of portfolio and project management practice since the 1980s-90s, drawing on the same value-versus-effort logic used in R&D and product roadmapping; no single credited originator, but closely related to project selection matrices taught in general strategy and PMI literature.
howToApply: List every initiative or option competing for time, budget, or attention.
Estimate each one's expected value or benefit if it succeeds — low or high.
Estimate each one's feasibility — how easy or hard it would be to pursue — low or high.
Plot each initiative into one of the four quadrants.
Fund high-value, high-feasibility initiatives first; investigate high-value, low-feasibility ones further; deprioritize the rest.
pros: Forces an explicit value-vs-effort tradeoff instead of funding by loudest voice or gut feel.
Works for portfolios of any size — a handful of projects or dozens.
Easy to redraw as priorities or feasibility estimates change.
cons: Two dimensions can't capture interdependencies between initiatives.
'Value' and 'feasibility' estimates are often rough guesses dressed up as data.
Says nothing about sequencing — several 'high/high' items can still compete for the same limited resources.

name: Feedback Analysis
description: Compares what you expected to happen when you made a decision against what actually happened, to sharpen your self-knowledge over time.
whenToUse: Use after a decision has played out and you want to learn from the gap between your prediction and the outcome, or before a similar decision to write your prediction down first.
origin: Popularized by management thinker Peter Drucker, who recommended writing down expected outcomes whenever making a key decision, then comparing results nine or twelve months later.
howToApply: Name the decision or action you took (or are about to take).
Write down specifically what you expected to happen, before or without looking at the outcome.
Record what actually happened.
Compare the two — where were you right, where were you wrong, and why.
Note what this reveals about your own judgment, blind spots, or strengths.
pros: Builds real self-knowledge from evidence, not vague self-impression.
Simple to start — just requires writing predictions down before results are known.
Compounds over time as a personal track record accumulates.
cons: Only useful in hindsight or with the discipline to write predictions down in advance.
Memory of 'what I expected' is unreliable unless actually recorded beforehand.
Doesn't tell you what to change, only that a gap exists.

result.summary: You consistently underestimate how long change takes to stick, even when the change itself turns out to be worth it.

name: Rubber Band Model
description: Looks at the stretch between where you are now and the vision or goal you're holding, and how that tension is likely to resolve.
whenToUse: Use when you feel a persistent pull toward a goal but haven't acted on it, or want to understand why motivation for a goal rises and falls.
origin: No single credited originator; the analogy of a stretched rubber band creating 'structural tension' between current reality and a held vision is common in goal-setting and creativity coaching literature, echoing ideas popularized by writers such as Robert Fritz.
howToApply: Name the vision or goal you're holding — where you want to be.
Describe current reality honestly — where you actually are right now.
Notice the tension this creates — restlessness, motivation, or avoidance.
Ask which way the tension is likely to resolve: will you move reality toward the vision, or quietly lower the vision toward reality?
Identify the smallest real action that moves reality, not the vision.
pros: Reframes uncomfortable tension as useful signal rather than something to escape.
Distinguishes real progress (moving reality) from quietly giving up (lowering the vision).
Works for almost any goal, personal or professional.
cons: Purely diagnostic — doesn't supply the action plan itself.
Can be uncomfortable to sit with tension rather than resolve it immediately.
Vague vision statements make the tension hard to feel or act on.

sections.body: Finishing a first draft of the book within the year.

sections.heading: Current Reality
sections.body: No consistent writing habit, a handful of scattered notes, over a year since starting.

sections.heading: The Tension
sections.body: The gap shows up as guilt and avoidance rather than motivation — a sign the vision may be getting quietly lowered instead of reality being moved.

result.summary: The tension is real, but right now it's resolving by shrinking the vision rather than growing the habit — a small, scheduled writing block would test which way it actually wants to go.

name: The Feedback Box
description: Structures difficult feedback into a clear sequence — situation, behavior, impact, and what you're asking for next — so it lands as useful rather than as an attack.
whenToUse: Use when preparing to give someone feedback on a specific behavior and want it to be concrete and actionable rather than vague or personal.
origin: A structured feedback approach closely related to the SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) model developed by the Center for Creative Leadership; no single individual is credited as the sole originator.
howToApply: Situation — name the specific time and place the behavior happened, not a generalization.
Behavior — describe exactly what the person did or said, observably, without interpretation.
Impact — explain the effect it had, on you, the team, or the outcome.
Ask — state clearly what you'd like to see instead, or ask an open question about their perspective.
pros: Keeps feedback concrete and specific instead of vague ('you're always...').
Separates observable behavior from interpretation, reducing defensiveness.
Ends with a clear ask instead of leaving the other person unsure what to do.
cons: Requires a specific, recent example on hand — vague discomfort doesn't fit the format.
Can feel scripted or clinical if delivered too rigidly.
Doesn't address patterns across many small incidents as easily as one clear moment.

example.scenario: Preparing to give a direct report feedback about interrupting colleagues in meetings.

steps.title: Behavior

steps.title: Impact
steps.description: They seemed to disengage for the rest of the meeting and didn't share the rest of their idea.

steps.title: Ask
steps.description: Could you try waiting for a pause before jumping in next time?

result.summary: Naming the specific meeting and moment makes this land as fixable feedback, not a character judgment.

name: Yes/No Rule
description: Tests your question against a simple rule — if it's not a clear 'hell yes,' it's a no — to cut through wishy-washy maybes.
whenToUse: Use when you're on the fence about a commitment and suspect you're talking yourself into something you're not genuinely excited about.
origin: Popularized by entrepreneur Derek Sivers as 'Hell Yeah or No' — if your reaction to an opportunity isn't an enthusiastic yes, treat it as a no.
howToApply: State the opportunity or commitment plainly.
List the reasons it could be a genuine 'Hell Yes.'
List the reasons it's actually a 'No' — including lukewarm or obligation-based reasons.
Notice which list is longer or more emotionally honest.
If it's not a clear Hell Yes, default to No.
pros: Cuts through decision fatigue by removing the 'maybe' option entirely.
Protects time and energy from being spread across half-hearted commitments.
Fast to apply — doesn't require elaborate analysis.
cons: Too blunt for decisions that are genuinely obligatory regardless of enthusiasm (taxes, caretaking).
Enthusiasm can be a poor predictor of long-term value for some choices.
Risk of using it to avoid anything that requires short-term discomfort for long-term gain.

name: Theory of Unconscious Thinking
description: Applies Unconscious Thought Theory to your question — deliberately stepping away from conscious deliberation so your non-conscious mind can process a complex decision with many variables.
whenToUse: Use for complex decisions with many competing factors, where you've already gathered the relevant information but conscious deliberation feels like it's going in circles.

Costs nothing but time.

Easy to use as an excuse to avoid a decision rather than genuinely process it.
Doesn't work for simple decisions with few variables — conscious deliberation is usually better there.

name: The Stop Rule

Makes the cost of continued searching explicit instead of invisible.
Reduces decision fatigue by pre-committing the stopping point.
cons: Setting the threshold itself requires judgment that can be wrong.
Can lead to settling prematurely if the bar is set too low.
Less useful for one-shot decisions with no ongoing search process.

name: The Making-of Model
description: Walks back through how a decision or piece of work actually got made — the intention behind it, the process you followed, the outcome, and the lesson — so you can learn from your own process, not just the result.
whenToUse: Use after a decision or project wraps up and you want to genuinely learn from how it went, not just whether it succeeded.

Works even when the outcome was good — most reflection models only trigger after failure.
Produces a specific, reusable lesson instead of a vague 'that went fine/badly.'
cons: Requires honest memory of your original intention, which can be rewritten in hindsight.
Easy to state a lesson too generic to actually change future behavior.
Best done soon after the fact — value fades if you wait too long to reflect.

name: Personal Potential Trap

name: The Hard Choice Model
description: Named after philosopher Ruth Chang's work on choices where the options are 'on a par' — not equal, not one clearly better, just genuinely incomparable — and what that means for how you should decide.
whenToUse: Use when you keep listing pros and cons but no option comes out clearly ahead, and the deadlock itself feels like the real problem.
origin: Based on philosopher Ruth Chang's work on hard choices and her widely-viewed TED talk 'How to Make Hard Choices,' which argues some choices are hard not because we lack information but because the options are on a par.
howToApply: Name the options that feel genuinely deadlocked.
Check whether one option is actually better, worse, or truly on a par with the other — not just hard to compare.

pros: Explains why more pro/con analysis sometimes makes a hard choice feel harder, not easier.

Can be misused to justify not doing real analysis on choices that do have a genuinely better option.
Requires a level of self-reflection ('who do I want to be') that's harder than comparing features.

name: Cognitive Bias Checklist
description: Scans your decision against well-documented cognitive biases from behavioral psychology and ranks which ones are most likely distorting your view of it right now.
whenToUse: Use when a decision feels obvious to you but you want a check on whether that certainty is earned or just a bias talking.
origin: Draws on the heuristics-and-biases research program led by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, popularized in Kahneman's 'Thinking, Fast and Slow.'

name: The Rumsfeld Matrix
description: Sorts what you know and don't know about your question into Known Knowns, Known Unknowns, Unknown Knowns, and Unknown Unknowns, to surface where your real uncertainty lies.
whenToUse: Use when a decision feels uncertain and you want to distinguish what you genuinely don't know from what you know but haven't articulated, or haven't even thought to ask.
origin: Popularized by U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld in a February 2002 press briefing, where he described 'known knowns,' 'known unknowns,' and 'unknown unknowns'; the fourth 'unknown knowns' quadrant was added later by commentators including philosopher Slavoj Žižek.
howToApply: State the decision and what's driving the uncertainty around it.

pros: Separates 'needs more research' (known unknowns) from 'needs more self-trust' (unknown knowns) — most models miss this second category.

Memorable phrasing makes it easy to reuse in conversation with others.
cons: Unknown unknowns are by definition hard to list — the quadrant can end up thin or generic.

name: The Swiss Cheese Model
description: Looks at the layers of defense protecting you against a specific failure, and where the holes in each layer might be lining up to let that failure through.

cons: Can be used to over-systematize what was actually a simple, single-cause failure.
Requires genuinely knowing your defense layers — hard to apply to novel or unfamiliar systems.

name: Maslow's Pyramid

whenToUse: Use when you're chasing a higher-level goal (like purpose or growth) while a more basic need is quietly unmet and undermining everything above it.

Simple, well-known structure that's easy to walk through quickly.
Applies to almost any personal question, not just career or work.
cons: The strict hierarchy (must satisfy lower levels before higher ones matter) is not well-supported by later research — needs often operate in parallel.

Doesn't tell you how to address a deficient level, only that it needs attention.

name: Bourdieu Model
description: Looks at why people occupy the social positions and make the choices they do, through habitus, capital, and field — Pierre Bourdieu's theory of social space.
whenToUse: Use when trying to understand why someone (or a group) thinks or acts differently than you'd expect, given their background.

Useful for understanding group dynamics, not just individual psychology.
cons: Abstract and academic — takes effort to translate into a concrete read on a specific situation.
Risk of using it to explain away disagreement rather than genuinely engage with someone's reasoning.
Requires real knowledge of someone's background, which you may not fully have.

name: Double Loop Learning

name: Appreciative Inquiry
description: Builds change on what's already working well, moving through Discover, Dream, Design, and Destiny, instead of starting from what's broken.
whenToUse: Use when coaching a person or team that's demoralized by a deficit-focused approach, or you want change to build on real strengths.
origin: Developed by David Cooperrider and Suresh Srivastva at Case Western Reserve University, first published in 1987.
howToApply: Discover — identify what's already working well and why.
Dream — envision what the best possible future looks like, building on those strengths.
Design — work out the concrete structures and practices that would make that future real.
Destiny — commit to specific next steps that sustain the change.
pros: Builds motivation and buy-in by starting from strength rather than deficit.
Good fit for team or culture work where morale is already fragile.
The 4-D structure is easy to run as a facilitated session.
cons: Can avoid necessary hard truths if used to dodge real problems.
Requires genuine strengths to build from — weak fit when the situation is genuinely broken.
The upbeat framing can feel forced if introduced without buy-in.

example.scenario: A team lead trying to rebuild morale after a rough quarter, without just papering over what went wrong.

steps.title: Discover
steps.description: The team shipped a hard release on time despite short staffing — surface what made that possible.

steps.title: Dream
steps.description: Imagine a quarter where that same resourcefulness isn't needed because workload is sustainable.

steps.title: Design
steps.description: Build a lightweight capacity-check into sprint planning based on what worked during the crunch.

steps.title: Destiny
steps.description: Commit to reviewing the capacity-check every sprint for the next quarter.

result.summary: Rebuilding from what the team proved it could do, not from what went wrong, gives the plan somewhere real to stand.

name: The Long Tail Model
description: Weighs a small number of big, obvious options against a long tail of niche ones that might collectively matter more than any single big option.
whenToUse: Use when you're tempted to chase the one obvious big option and want to check whether a portfolio of smaller bets serves you better.
origin: Coined by Chris Anderson in a 2004 Wired article, later expanded into his 2006 book 'The Long Tail'.
howToApply: List the big, obvious options (the head) relevant to your question.
List the smaller, niche options (the tail) that are individually minor but numerous.
Estimate the realistic payoff of each, weighing likelihood alongside size.
Rank all options together, not head vs tail separately.
Decide whether concentrating on the head or spreading across the tail actually serves your goal.
pros: Prevents overlooking niche options that collectively add up to more than the obvious big one.
Useful corrective when 'go big or go home' thinking is the default.
Forces an honest side-by-side ranking instead of assuming big automatically means best.
cons: Chasing too many small bets can spread effort too thin to execute any of them well.
Requires real estimation of the tail's collective payoff, which is often uncertain.
Not every decision has a meaningful tail — can be forced onto situations that don't fit.

example.scenario: A solo creator deciding whether to chase one big sponsorship deal or build several smaller income streams.

items.label: Several smaller recurring sponsors
items.rationale: More resilient, less dependent on any single relationship

items.label: One big sponsorship deal
items.rationale: Highest single payoff but concentrated risk

items.label: Niche paid community
items.rationale: Small now but compounds over time

result.summary: The combined tail options edge out the single big deal on both payoff and resilience.

name: Conflict Resolution Model
description: Maps a conflict onto the five Thomas-Kilmann styles so you can choose a resolution approach deliberately instead of defaulting to habit.
whenToUse: Use when navigating a disagreement and unsure whether to push, yield, or find middle ground.
origin: Based on the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument, developed by Kenneth Thomas and Ralph Kilmann in the 1970s.
howToApply: Name the conflict and what's at stake for each side.
Consider Competing — pursuing your own concerns at the other's expense.
Consider Collaborating — working together to fully satisfy both sides.
Consider Compromising — each side gives up something for a middle ground.
Consider Avoiding and Accommodating as the remaining two styles.
Choose the style that fits how much you care about the relationship versus the outcome here.
pros: Names five distinct approaches instead of defaulting to whichever one is habitual.
Makes explicit the trade-off between relationship and outcome that's often left implicit.
Widely taught, so it's easy to discuss with the other party using shared language.
cons: Doesn't tell you which style is right for a given conflict — that judgment call remains yours.
People often default to one style regardless of situation, and naming it doesn't automatically change that.
Oversimplifies conflicts that don't cleanly map to a single style.

example.scenario: Deciding how to handle a disagreement with a co-founder over the company's spending pace.

rows.label: Competing
items: Push hard for your budget position
Risks damaging the co-founder relationship

rows.label: Collaborating
items: Dig into both sets of concerns together
Slower but likely to produce a better shared plan

rows.label: Compromising
items: Split the difference on spend
Fast but may satisfy neither position fully

result.summary: Given the long-term partnership at stake, Collaborating is worth the extra time here.

name: The Black Swan Model
description: Looks at your question through the lens of rare, high-impact, hard-to-predict events, and how exposed you are to one.
whenToUse: Use when a decision has a small chance of an extreme outcome that ordinary planning tends to ignore.
origin: Developed by Nassim Nicholas Taleb, most fully in his 2007 book 'The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable'.
howToApply: Name the decision and its normal, expected range of outcomes.
Ask what rare, extreme event — positive or negative — sits outside that expected range.
Assess how exposed you currently are if that rare event happened.
Ask whether you can cheaply reduce your downside exposure or increase your upside exposure to that event.
Favor decisions with limited downside and open-ended upside over the reverse.
pros: Corrects for the common mistake of planning only around the expected or average case.
Reframes risk in terms of exposure and fragility, not just probability.
Encourages asymmetric bets — limited downside, open upside — which compound well over time.
cons: Can tip into excessive worry about unlikely events that never materialize.
Hard to act on precisely, since black swans are by definition hard to predict.
Risk of using it to justify inaction rather than genuine risk management.

example.scenario: Deciding whether to keep all savings in a single employer's stock plan.

sections.heading: Expected Range
sections.body: Under normal conditions, the stock plan performs roughly in line with the market.

sections.heading: The Black Swan
sections.body: A rare company-specific failure could wipe out both your job and your savings at the same time.

sections.heading: Exposure and Fix
sections.body: The correlated risk — losing income and savings together — is the real danger, and it's cheap to fix by diversifying savings outside the employer.

result.summary: The risk isn't the stock's average performance, it's the rare scenario where job and savings fail together — diversify to remove that correlation.

name: Crossing the Chasm
description: Places your question on the technology or idea adoption curve, from early enthusiasts to the mainstream, to spot where the hard part actually is.
whenToUse: Use when trying to grow adoption of a new product, idea, or practice beyond its earliest supporters.
origin: Developed by Geoffrey Moore in his 1991 book 'Crossing the Chasm', building on Everett Rogers' 1962 Diffusion of Innovation theory.
howToApply: Identify where your current adopters sit on the curve: Innovators, Early Adopters, Early Majority, Late Majority, or Laggards.
Name the chasm — the gap between visionary early adopters and the pragmatic early majority.
Assess what's needed to appeal to the more risk-averse early majority, not just more of what worked with early adopters.
Identify a narrow beachhead segment within the early majority to target first.
Plan the specific move that gets you across the chasm rather than just growing within the early-adopter segment.
pros: Explains why growth often stalls even when early enthusiasm was strong.
Forces a distinct strategy for crossing to the mainstream, rather than just more marketing.
Widely used framework, easy to communicate to stakeholders.
cons: Originally built for tech products — translates less cleanly to non-product ideas or personal decisions.
Assumes a fairly linear adoption curve, which doesn't fit every situation.
Identifying your specific beachhead segment is hard and easy to get wrong.

example.scenario: A startup with an enthusiastic niche user base trying to figure out why broader growth has stalled.

steps.title: Innovators
steps.description: A handful of technical users adopted early purely for the novelty.

steps.title: Early Adopters
steps.description: A visionary segment adopted for the strategic advantage, tolerating rough edges.

steps.title: The Chasm
steps.description: Growth has stalled because the product still requires early-adopter patience the pragmatic majority won't give it.

steps.title: Early Majority Beachhead
steps.description: Target one narrow, pragmatic use case with a polished, low-effort onboarding to cross the gap.

result.summary: The stall is the chasm, not a marketing problem — narrow the target and polish onboarding before pushing broader growth.

name: The Black Box Model
description: Treats a system as Input, an unexamined internal Process, and Output — useful when you can observe results but not the mechanism producing them.
whenToUse: Use when you need to make a decision about a system you can observe but don't fully understand the internals of.
origin: A general systems-thinking concept with no single credited inventor; the black-box framing traces to control theory and cybernetics work in the mid-20th century, notably associated with Norbert Wiener's cybernetics.
howToApply: Name the system and what you can actually observe going in (inputs) and coming out (outputs).
Acknowledge what you genuinely don't know about the internal process.
Look for patterns between specific inputs and specific outputs across multiple observations.
Use those input-output patterns to make decisions without needing to fully understand the mechanism.
Note where the black-box approach breaks down and real understanding of the internals would actually help.
pros: Lets you act on a system pragmatically without needing full understanding first.
Focuses attention on what's actually observable rather than speculative internals.
Useful for complex systems (organizations, markets, other people) where full transparency isn't realistic.
cons: Can mask genuine understanding you actually need for a high-stakes decision.
Pattern-matching on inputs and outputs alone can mislead if the underlying process isn't stable.
Not a substitute for investigating the internals when that's actually feasible and worthwhile.

sections.heading: Input
sections.body: Pitches that led to approval were all short, numbers-first, and sent before Friday.

sections.heading: Process
sections.body: The internal reasoning behind their decisions is not visible or shared.

sections.heading: Output
sections.body: Every pitch matching that pattern was approved; every longer, narrative-first pitch stalled.

result.summary: Without knowing why, matching the observed pattern — short, numbers-first, early in the week — is still a rational bet.

name: The Prisoner's Dilemma
description: Frames a decision involving another person or party as a game-theory standoff, showing how mutual cooperation and mutual self-interest can produce very different outcomes for both sides.
whenToUse: Use when your outcome depends on how another party responds, and you're tempted to act purely in your own short-term interest.
origin: Formalized by Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher at RAND Corporation in 1950, with the 'prisoner' framing and its name added shortly after by Albert Tucker.
howToApply: Name the other party and the decision you both face.
Describe what happens if you both cooperate.
Describe what happens if you both defect (act purely in self-interest).
Describe what happens if one cooperates and the other defects.
Notice whether short-term self-interest is quietly steering you toward a worse outcome for both of you.
Decide whether signaling cooperation first could shift the dynamic.
pros: Makes an invisible dynamic explicit — you see the payoff structure, not just your own instinct.
Explains why rational self-interest can produce a worse outcome for everyone, including you.
Useful shorthand for negotiations, partnerships, and repeated relationships.
cons: Real situations rarely have cleanly defined, symmetric payoffs like the textbook version.
Assumes both parties are acting rationally on the same information, which is often false.
Can overintellectualize what's really a trust or communication problem.

example.scenario: Deciding whether to share your roadmap openly with a close competitor who's proposed an informal information-sharing arrangement.

rows.label: If they cooperate
items: You both share roadmaps and each avoid duplicated bets
Best combined outcome, but only works if trust holds

rows.label: If they defect
items: They gain a copy of your roadmap while giving you nothing back
Worst outcome for you if you cooperated and they didn't

result.summary: The single-shot temptation to defect is real, but this is a repeated relationship — signal cooperation cautiously and watch how they respond before sharing anything sensitive.

name: The Team Model
description: Walks a group through Bruce Tuckman's five stages of team development, so you can name which stage your team is actually in and what that implies.
whenToUse: Use when a team feels stuck, is newly formed, or is going through a rough patch, and you want to understand the dynamic instead of just reacting to it.
origin: Developed by psychologist Bruce Tuckman in 1965 ('Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing'); the fifth stage, Adjourning, was added in 1977 with Mary Ann Jensen.
howToApply: Describe the team and the situation you're trying to understand.
Forming — are people still polite, cautious, and unclear on roles?
Storming — is there visible friction, competing ideas, or pushback on direction?
Norming — are norms and roles starting to settle, with more trust?
Performing — is the team working effectively with minimal friction?
Adjourning — is the team winding down or dispersing, and does that need acknowledging?
pros: Normalizes conflict as a stage, not a sign of failure — Storming is expected, not fatal.
Gives a shared vocabulary for a team to name what's happening to it.
Simple enough to revisit quickly whenever team dynamics shift.
cons: Real teams don't move through the stages in a clean line — they loop back, especially after a membership change.
Doesn't say how to move a team from one stage to the next, just what stage it's in.
Can be used to dismiss real problems as 'just Storming' when something more serious is wrong.

example.scenario: A newly merged team from two departments still deferring to each other too politely three weeks in, with unclear ownership starting to cause friction.

steps.title: Forming
steps.description: Everyone is polite and roles are still unclear — this describes where the team likely started.

steps.title: Storming
steps.description: Ownership friction is starting to surface as people push back on unclear responsibilities.

steps.title: Norming
steps.description: Needs explicit role clarification to move past the friction into agreed norms.

steps.title: Performing
steps.description: Only reachable once roles and trust are settled — not yet.

result.summary: The team is exiting Forming and entering Storming — naming ownership explicitly now will speed the move into Norming.

name: The Hersey-Blanchard Model
description: Matches a leadership style to how much direction and support a specific person needs on a specific task, rather than applying one leadership style to everyone.
whenToUse: Use when deciding how hands-on or hands-off to be with someone you're managing or mentoring on a particular task.
origin: Developed by Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard in the late 1960s as Situational Leadership Theory.
howToApply: Name the person and the specific task or responsibility in question.
Assess their competence on this task — low or high.
Assess their commitment or confidence on this task — low or high.
Match to a style: Directing, Coaching, Supporting, or Delegating.
Adjust your behavior deliberately rather than defaulting to your usual style.
pros: Explicitly ties leadership style to the person and task, not a fixed personal philosophy.
Gives permission to be more hands-on with someone without it meaning you don't trust them generally.
Simple enough to reassess quickly as someone grows into a role.
cons: Assessing someone's true competence and commitment is subjective and easy to get wrong.
Can be used to justify micromanaging under the label of 'Directing'.
Says nothing about how to actually build the skill or confidence you're waiting for.

quadrants.name: Supporting

quadrants.name: Delegating
items: Target for once they've run one project end-to-end

result.summary: Start in Coaching mode now, and plan to shift to Supporting after their first project milestone.

name: The Role-Playing Model
description: Has you mentally step into another person's position to work out how they're likely thinking, before you decide how to approach them.
whenToUse: Use before a difficult conversation, negotiation, or decision that heavily involves predicting someone else's reaction.
origin: No single credited originator — a general perspective-taking technique drawn from psychology, negotiation training, and role-play practice used broadly across coaching and mediation.
howToApply: Name the other person and the situation.
Step into their position — what do they want, and what are they afraid of here?
Consider what information or pressure they have that you don't.
Predict how they'd likely react to your intended approach.
Adjust your approach based on what that reveals.
pros: Surfaces reactions you wouldn't have predicted from your own perspective alone.
Cheap and fast — no need to actually involve the other person to get value from it.
Builds general empathy skill with repeated use.
cons: You're still guessing — it's your model of them, not their actual perspective.
Can lead to false confidence if you mistake your simulation for real understanding.
Doesn't replace actually asking them directly when that's an option.

name: Result Optimisation Model
description: Identifies which specific levers are most likely to move a particular outcome, and ranks them by expected impact so effort goes to the highest-leverage ones first.
whenToUse: Use when you have a clear target outcome and multiple possible levers, and need to know which ones are actually worth pulling.
origin: No single credited originator — a general framing drawn from decision analysis and optimization practice.
howToApply: State the specific result you're trying to improve.
List every lever that could plausibly move that result.
Estimate each lever's likely impact.
Rank levers from highest to lowest expected impact.
Commit effort to the top few before spreading thin across all of them.
pros: Forces explicit prioritization instead of working every lever equally.
Makes the reasoning behind priority visible and arguable, not just intuition.
Reusable for almost any outcome-improvement question.
cons: Impact estimates are often rough guesses dressed up as numbers.
Ignores effort or cost required to pull each lever, only ranks impact.
Can undervalue levers with compounding, slow-building effects.

result.summary: Fix the headline first — it's the highest-leverage, lowest-effort change available.

name: The Project Management Triangle
description: Names the three constraints — scope, time, and cost — that trade off against each other on any project, and scores how much pressure each is under right now.
whenToUse: Use when a project feels squeezed and you need to see which constraint is actually being pushed, and what that implies for the others.
origin: Commonly attributed to Martin Barnes, who is credited with articulating the 'iron triangle' of project constraints around 1969.
howToApply: Name the project and what's prompting the question.
Score how much pressure Scope is under right now (0-10).
Score how much pressure Time is under right now (0-10).
Score how much pressure Cost is under right now (0-10).
Accept that pushing on one constraint will pull on at least one of the others.
Decide deliberately which constraint you're willing to flex.
pros: Makes trade-offs explicit instead of pretending you can improve all three at once.
Quick shared language for stakeholders arguing past each other about a squeezed project.
Forces a deliberate choice about which constraint absorbs the pressure.
cons: Oversimplifies real projects, which have more than three relevant dimensions (e.g. quality, risk).
Doesn't say how to actually manage the trade-off, just names that one exists.
Can be used to excuse poor planning as an inevitable trade-off.

result.summary: Scope has grown without releasing Time or Cost — something has to give, most realistically the deadline.

name: The Drexler-Sibbet Team Performance Model
description: Diagnoses which of seven stages a team is in on its way to (or away from) high performance, from initial Orientation through to Renewal.
whenToUse: Use when a team's performance seems stuck and you want a more granular diagnosis than 'we're just not gelling'.
origin: Developed by Allan Drexler and David Sibbet, building on earlier team-development research, and published as the Team Performance Model in the 1980s.
howToApply: Name the team and the concern prompting the question.
Orientation — is there still confusion about why the team exists?
Trust Building — is there enough psychological safety to be candid?
Goal Clarification — are goals and roles genuinely clear and agreed?
Commitment — has the team actually committed to a plan, or just discussed one?
Implementation — is execution happening smoothly?
High Performance — is the team exceeding expectations?
Renewal — does the team need to revisit its purpose after a change?
pros: More granular than most team-stage models, useful for pinpointing exactly where things stall.
Distinguishes 'trust' and 'clarity' problems, which need very different fixes.
Includes Renewal, acknowledging teams need periodic re-founding, not just formation once.
cons: Seven stages is a lot to hold in mind compared to simpler models.
Diagnosing which stage a team is 'really' in is still a judgment call.
Less widely known, so it takes more effort to introduce to a team as shared language.

steps.title: Goal Clarification

steps.title: Commitment

steps.title: Implementation
steps.description: Execution is inconsistent because commitment underneath it is shaky.

steps.title: High Performance
steps.description: Not reachable until commitment is genuinely secured.

result.summary: The team likely skipped real Commitment on the way to Implementation — worth revisiting explicitly.

name: The Expectations Model
description: Breaks down what's really driving (or undermining) someone's motivation into three factors: whether effort leads to performance, performance leads to reward, and whether the reward is actually valued.
whenToUse: Use when someone (including yourself) seems unmotivated and you want to know which specific link in the chain is broken.
origin: Developed by Victor Vroom in his 1964 book 'Work and Motivation', known as Expectancy Theory.
howToApply: Name the person and the behavior or effort in question.
Assess Expectancy — do they believe effort will actually lead to good performance?
Assess Instrumentality — do they believe good performance will actually lead to the reward?
Assess Valence — do they actually value that reward?
Identify which of the three is weakest — that's the real motivation gap.
pros: Pinpoints exactly which link in the motivation chain is broken instead of a vague 'they're not motivated'.
Applies equally well to understanding your own stalled motivation.
Prevents wasted effort — no point improving rewards if the real issue is that effort doesn't feel connected to performance.
cons: Requires honest insight into someone's beliefs, which can be hard to assess from outside.
Assumes fairly rational, calculated motivation, which doesn't capture every source of drive.
Doesn't address motivation rooted in identity, habit, or emotion rather than expected payoff.

example.scenario: A normally strong performer has been visibly coasting on a project for weeks.

sections.heading: Expectancy
sections.body: They likely still believe effort translates to good work — their skill hasn't wavered.

sections.heading: Instrumentality
sections.body: The real gap: recent decisions on this project were made without their input, so performance may not feel connected to influence over the outcome.
